title: Breathing, read whole
hook: the sixteen steps fulfill the four foundations and the seven factors

segments.voice: Yesterday: samma ditthi, right view first among the great forty, and your line, view leads.

You've met the breath on this path many times: one breath with the bell, three breaths, long and short. Pieces. Today, the whole thing. The hundred and eighteenth discourse is set at the Eastern Park near Savatthi. The rains retreat should be ending, but the Buddha is so pleased with his monks that he stays another month, until the next full moon. New monks arrive to learn, and senior monks teach them, ten, twenty, thirty, forty students each. And on that full-moon night, the Buddha teaches mindfulness of breathing from start to finish.
screen: `ONE BREATH. THREE. LONG AND SHORT.` → `THE MONKS STAY ANOTHER MONTH.` → `THE WHOLE TEACHING, ONE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: It's called anapanasati: mindfulness of in-breath and out-breath. You go to a forest, the root of a tree or an empty hut, sit with the body upright, and set mindfulness in front of you. Then come sixteen steps, in four sets of four. The first four are the body. Breathing in long, you know it's long; breathing in short, you know it's short. You train to breathe in experiencing the whole body, and calming the body. The second four are feeling: breathing with joy, with ease, knowing how feelings shape the mind, and calming that. The third four are the mind: knowing it, gladdening it, steadying it, releasing it. The last four are what you see: impermanence, fading, ending, letting go. Then the big claim. These sixteen steps, the Buddha says, fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness, body, feeling, mind and phenomena, one set of four each. The four foundations, practiced well, fulfill the seven factors of awakening: mindfulness, investigation, energy, joy, calm, concentration and equanimity. And those seven, fulfilled, bring true knowledge and release. One breath, followed all the way, carries the entire path. That's a big promise about something you do some twenty thousand times a day without noticing. Nothing in it needs a special tool. Only the next breath.
screen: `ANAPANASATI: MINDFUL BREATHING` · `SIXTEEN STEPS IN FOUR FOURS` · `THE FOUR FOUNDATIONS FULFILLED` · `SEVEN FACTORS, THEN RELEASE` · then, large: `THE BREATH DOES IT ALL.`

segments.voice: Sit upright: breathing in long, know it's long; breathing in short, know it's short. Then breathe in and out feeling the whole body, and if it settles, let each in-breath calm the body a little more.
Breathing. Anapanasati: sixteen steps that fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness, the seven factors of awakening, and release.
Your line: the breath does it all. The whole path rides on the next breath. Day four eighty-eight, done.

howItsDone: Mindfulness of breathing is one of the most widely taught meditations across Theravada, Zen and Tibetan schools, and many teachers lead students through the sixteen steps of MN 118, often over weeks of retreat.

what a scholar hears: the Anapanasati Sutta maps its four tetrads onto the four satipatthanas, and those onto the seven bojjhangas, an explicit chain inside one discourse.

notes: MN 118 paraphrased. Confirm the setting: Eastern Park, Migara's mother's palace; the Buddha extends his stay to the Komudi full moon of the fourth month; senior monks teaching ten, twenty, thirty, forty new monks.
The 'twenty thousand times a day' figure is a rough everyday estimate of human breathing, not from the text; remove if a Keeper prefers.
The outline practice asks for fifteen minutes; the script offers two with the bell and invites more later.
Audit (10% sample): the practice referred to 'the outline', which the listener never sees; MN 118 seats the Buddha in the open air, so 'a room full of monks' was corrected.
